projects.org_note: Numbers track Evžen Wybitul as an individual (solo Master's student at ETH Zurich at proposal time), not any org. This specific project closed 'not funded' with $0 raised and zero transactions on Manifund. However, Wybitul attended ICML anyway (self-funded plus a $1,000 grant from the workshop itself) and refiled the same ask as a sibling Manifund project, slug 'retroactive-presenting-a-poster-at-the-icml-technical-ai-governance-workshop', which raised $1,300 from Ryan Kidd on 2025-11-24 (Manifund money, so excluded from external_funding and from this slug's manifund_raised_by_year). Other context found: he did the Talos AI Governance Fellowship and started a funded DPhil at Oxford's AIMS CDT (per aigi.ox.ac.uk/people/evzen-wybitul/) — the studentship presumably covers fees+stipend but no public dollar amount, so no entry recorded. Pre-window (2024): as part of Team Shard he shared an LTFF 6-month stipend grant (with Alex Cloud, Jacob Goldman-Wetzler, Joseph Miller) for gradient routing, plus Neel Nanda/Manifund compute funding, per his own proposal text; amounts not published, and it predates the 2025 window. Searches: name+grant, name+LTFF/EA Funds payouts, LTFF payout report pages, Oxford/Talos bio pages.
projects.research_summary: The original proposal expired unfunded, but Wybitul attended ICML 2025 in Vancouver anyway, presenting his solo paper on verification-based access controls at the TAIG workshop. He covered costs with personal funds plus a $1,000 travel grant from the workshop, and in November 2025 recouped the remaining $1,300 via a retroactive Manifund project funded by Ryan Kidd. He has since transitioned into technical AI governance: he completed the Talos AI Governance Fellowship and began a DPhil at Oxford's AIMS CDT, filing a final report in May 2026 confirming the trip served its career-transition purpose.

projects.research_summary: The project received no Manifund donations and no traceable external funding through August 2026. No evidence was found that the pending Emergent Ventures or Nonlinear applications mentioned in the proposal resulted in grants, and the project has no discoverable public footprint (no papers, repos in search results, press, or grantee listings) after the proposal.

Major external support arrived via SFF ($343k in 2024; $70k + $206k matching pledge in 2025) and a $1.557M Open Philanthropy/Coefficient Giving operating-expenses grant in January 2025, plus UK AISI funding of undisclosed size.

Manifund itself put in ~$500k of internal subsidy ('Grant funding (Manifund): $500k' per the one-year retrospective) — that is Manifund's own money, not external, and is excluded from external_funding. Mox also generated ~$600k in earned revenue (memberships/offices/events) through early 2026, which is revenue, not grants. The Feb 2026 EA Forum post says Mox 'raised in total $550k' in year 1 against a $1.6M minimal budget. projects.research_summary: Mox launched Feb 15, 2025 as a 20,000 sq ft, 2-floor coworking and events space in SF and became the city's largest AI safety / EA community hub. It fell well short of its year-1 funding tiers ($1.6M-$3.6M), raising ~$550k in grants (Manifund subsidy $500k counted separately; Craig Falls & EAIF $300k combined) while generating ~$600k of earned revenue. In Feb 2026 it opened a year-2 fundraiser seeking $450k (deployable up to $1.2M), projecting $1.4M in 2026 revenue.

projects.research_summary: The documentary filmed through 2025 (interviews include Geoffrey Hinton and Yoshua Bengio), raised ~$205k on Manifund plus off-platform money ('well over $300,000' total by June 2025 per Axiotes), then pivoted from donations to private film financing. A post-production Manifund page targeting $327.5k raised almost nothing, but by July 15, 2026 Axiotes announced the film was fully financed at project level with a $1.6M ring-fenced budget via a private investment raise, closed the Manifund page to donations, and is aiming for festivals and streamer acquisition (Netflix/Amazon/Apple TV+), with release expected later in 2026.

projects.research_summary: After the Dec 2023 'this might be the last AI Safety Camp' funding crisis, the 10th edition was funded (~$103k: $68.5k Manifund, $30k SFF speculation grants, $7.5k private) and ran January-April 2025 with ~30 projects. The program continued: an 11th edition fundraise followed on Manifund, and in the SFF-2025 S-Process round AI Safety Camp received $200,000 general support (via Ashgro Inc.) plus a conditional $110,000 matching pledge.

Total funding received was ~$143k: ~$119k via Manifund donations, $4k via a Ryan Kidd Manifund regrant on another project, and $20k from the Future of Life Institute; Trazzi covered the remaining gap and published a detailed post-mortem in mid-2025.

projects.org_note: Numbers track Forethought (forethought.org, aka Forethought Research), the AI macrostrategy nonprofit cofounded mid-2024 by Max Dalton, Will MacAskill, Tom Davidson, and Amrit Sidhu-Brar — not the older, unrelated Forethought Foundation for Global Priorities Research or the Forethought AI startup. The Manifund page was one channel of their org-wide 2025-26 fundraiser (ask $2.4M baseline / $3.9M expansion through June 2027; baseline goal met by March 2026). Their startup funding through ~March 2026 came from two undisclosed high-net-worth donors with no public amounts. Longview Philanthropy and Coefficient Giving (formerly Open Philanthropy) have evaluated and endorsed Forethought and recommend it to their donor networks, but I could not verify any direct grant from either (Coefficient Giving's grants database returned 403 to automated fetch; web searches found no grant page). 2026 baseline budget is $4.1M, so most of what they raised beyond Manifund + SFF is unattributable to specific funders/amounts.
projects.research_summary: Forethought launched publicly in March 2025 as an AI macrostrategy research group and published 20+ papers (including the AI-enabled coups work) in its first year. Its Dec 2025 Manifund proposal was part of an org-wide fundraiser; the baseline goal ($2.4M for operations through June 2027) was fulfilled by March 2026, including $365k via Manifund led by Neel Nanda ($200k) and Ethan Perez ($100k). It also received a $103k SFF-2025 general-support grant and planned another funding round in August 2026 for expenses through June 2028.

external_funding.note: 6-month research stipend for AI alignment research on circuits in decision transformers. Granted Feb 2023 (reported April 2023), i.e. a few months BEFORE the July 2023 Manifund proposal, but within the proposal year.

projects.org_note: Numbers track Joseph Bloom as an individual independent researcher (this project), not Decode Research/Neuronpedia, the nonprofit he later cofounded, which raised separately (LTFF ~1yr of Neuronpedia funding, Open Philanthropy, Anthropic, AISTOF, and its own Manifund project 'neuronpedia---ai-safety-game'). Searches tried: LTFF/EA Funds payout reports for 'Joseph Bloom'; 'Joseph Bloom Lightspeed Grants amount'; Open Phil/Coefficient grants DB for 'Decode Research'/'Neuronpedia'; his CV PDF (no funding section); SFF 2025 recommendations (no Decode/Neuronpedia grant).
projects.research_summary: After raising $51.4k on Manifund in mid-2023, Bloom received a Lightspeed grant extending his independent runway, pivoted from decision-transformer circuits to sparse autoencoders (releasing SAELens and open-source residual-stream SAEs), cofounded the nonprofit Decode Research around Neuronpedia (which partnered with DeepMind on Gemma Scope), and subsequently joined the UK AI Security Institute as Head of Model Transparency.

projects.org_note: Numbers track this specific 4-person MATS 6.0 scholar team (Alex Cloud, Jacob Goldman-Wetzler, Evžen Wybitul, Joseph Miller; mentor Alex Turner), not any organization. Manifund ask was fully funded in one $16,047 donation by regrantor Neel Nanda (Aug 2024). Outcome: 'Gradient Routing: Masking Gradients to Localize Computation in Neural Networks' (arXiv:2410.04332); Manifund funds were credited as critical for Table 1 results; submitted to ICLR 2025 then resubmitted to ICML. The team's LTFF $160k covered 6-month post-MATS stipends; they had also applied to FAR AI, with no public record of a resulting grant found. Alex Cloud subsequently joined Anthropic (co-author of the 2025 subliminal learning paper) — employment, not grant funding.

Numbers track a pseudonymous individual, 'H' — a researcher accepted to a UK Computer Science PhD program, with prior work with UK DSIT, Oxford Martin School, GovAI, CSER, and IAPS. The single $87,543 Manifund donation came from JueYan Zhang's AI Safety Tactical Opportunities Fund (AISTOF), which is a regrant made ON Manifund, not external funding. Because the creator is pseudonymous, external funding is essentially untraceable: searched (1) the project topic + Manifund/PhD funding, (2) pseudonymous researcher + affiliations (DSIT, GovAI, CSER, IAPS, global majority), (3) AISTOF public grant lists, and (4) AI-governance PhD scholarship/fellowship announcements 2025-2026. No external grants attributable to this person were found; the project notes H was ineligible for UK student loans, consistent with no other funding at proposal time.
projects.research_summary: H, a pseudonymous researcher, was fully funded in a single $87,543 AISTOF regrant (via JueYan Zhang) on 2025-07-22 to cover first-year UK PhD tuition (~£33,370), living expenses (~£24,420), and visa fees (~£6,500) for research on frontier AI governance inclusive of the global majority. Because the recipient is pseudonymous, there is no public post-grant trail; no external funding to this individual could be identified.

projects.org_note: External funding tracks CeSIA (Centre pour la Sécurité de l'IA / French Center for AI Safety, a French nonprofit that grew out of EffiSciences' AI division) as an organization — the Manifund project funded only one specific program (content-creator advisory work, ~1 FTE). No quantified external grants were found within the window (proposal year 2025 through Aug 2026). Known pre-window grants: SFF-2024 recommended $48,000 (funder Jaan Tallinn, receiving charity EffiSciences, 'General support of CeSIA', https://survivalandflourishing.fund/recommendations) and Effektiv Spenden's Safeguarding the Future fund ~€195,000 (H1/2024 allocation, disbursed Sept 2024, https://effektiv-spenden.org/en/safeguarding-the-future/). CeSIA's Dec 2024 announcement also lists Longview Philanthropy, AISTOF, a Swedish foundation, Erasmus+, and Ryan Kidd via Manifund as funders without amounts (https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/rCLs56wfissFheLap/announcing-cesia-the-french-center-for-ai-safety). For 2025-2026, CeSIA's site (https://cesia.org/en/about/) says it is funded by the European Commission, ENS, UK AI Security Institute (UK AISI), and European/British philanthropies — the UK AISI and some EC funding likely falls in-window, but no amounts or dates are public, so no entries were recorded. CeSIA/EffiSciences does NOT appear in SFF-2025 recommendations, and no Coefficient Giving (Open Philanthropy) or LTFF/EA Funds grants to CeSIA were found.
projects.research_summary: CeSIA fully funded this project on Manifund ($21,309 vs a $21,000 goal, June 2025) and continued growing as France's main AI safety org through 2025-2026: advising on the French national AI evaluation lab, participating in the EU GPAI Code of Practice and UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance, and continuing creator-advisory work (e.g., the Ego video with 4M+ views predated the ask). Its disclosed 2025-2026 funders are the European Commission, ENS, UK AISI, and European/British philanthropies, but no public grant amounts in that window could be verified; its major quantified grants (SFF $48k; Effektiv Spenden ~€195k) date to 2024, before the proposal.

projects.research_summary: Apart Research kept operating and growing after the Dec 2023 proposal: it received a $294k SFF grant in 2024 and self-reported $500k+ raised in 2024 from LTFF, Foresight Institute, and ACX Grants. In spring 2025 an LTFF pass left it with a funding crisis; a public 'Help Save Apart' campaign sought $954,800 and closed at about $620k, keeping the org alive. As of Nov 2025 it was still active (EA Forum Marginal Funding Week post), running hackathons, the Studio, and Fellowship programs, with research used by Anthropic, UK AISI, and the EU AI Office.

Berman remained active in AI-risk advocacy: he continued grassroots lobbying of Congress with PauseAI US and published the 2025 book 'Catastrophe: The Unstoppable Threat of AI' (following 'AI Endgame'), and appeared on the For Humanity podcast.

rubrics.name: Survival and Flourishing Fund (SFF)
rubrics.thesis:
SFF exists to "support the long-term survival and flourishing of sentient life," and in practice the large majority of its money goes to reducing existential risk from advanced AI. It is not a foundation with a program staff and a house view; it is a grant-recommendation *process* run for its funders — overwhelmingly Jaan Tallinn (Skype co-founder), with additional funders like Jed McCaleb and the Future of Life Institute. Since 2019 it has coordinated roughly $152M in gifts, and in recent years distributes on the order of $30–40M per year across ~90–100 organizations.

The worldview anchoring the money is Tallinn's: his stated goal is to "maintain and improve humanity's ability to exist and enjoy existing," with the current decade's focus on AI extinction risk. He favors **restrictive measures** on frontier AI — datacenter certification and international oversight, legally mandated speed limits on AI computation, liability laws (including "Know Your Developer" for open-source), mandatory labeling of AI interactions, veto committees for large deployments, and global off-switch capacity — alongside **constructive measures**: collective-intelligence tools for human cooperation, guaranteed-safe AI with quantifiable safety specs, hardware-level controls, and AI for healthcare. SFF rounds since 2024 have also run explicit **Freedom** (avoiding concentration of power, protecting speech and individual liberty) and **Fairness** (AI empowering the disempowered, resisting monopoly, inclusive governance) tracks, and 2026 added theme rounds in climate change, animal welfare, and human enhancement — but the Main Track (AI x-risk broadly) gets the large majority of dollars.

Culturally, SFF's recommenders are drawn from the rationalist/x-risk community (past and current recommenders include Zvi Mowshowitz, Nate Soares, Malo Bourgon, Scott Alexander, Oliver Habryka, Eliezer Yudkowsky as a Speculator), so proposals are read by people who take AGI ruin scenarios seriously, are skeptical of pure capabilities-adjacent work, and reward legible theories of change about x-risk reduction — technical alignment research, AI governance and policy advocacy (including "slow down / regulate" advocacy that other funders shy away from), field-building like MATS, and biosecurity (e.g. SecureDNA). The S-Process is explicitly designed "to generally favor funding things that at least one Recommender is excited to fund, rather than things that every Recommender is excited to fund" — so a proposal that strongly excites one credible evaluator can win even if others are lukewarm, which makes SFF friendlier to weird, speculative, or contrarian bets than consensus-driven funders. What it avoids: individuals without fiscal sponsors (orgs only), work outside the survival-and-flourishing frame, and — per Tallinn — things outside his stated priorities (with carve-out exceptions for climate and life extension). Grants range from ~$5k to ~$1.6M per round, so it writes many mid-six-figure checks rather than a few mega-grants.

rubrics.typical_check_size: Roughly $5k–$1.6M per org per round; median around $150k–$250k. SFF-2024: largest $1.62M (Center for AI Safety Action Fund), smallest $5k (Foxglove). SFF-2025: largest $1.5M (SecureDNA), smallest ~$16k. Speculation Grants are typically ≤$400k (each Speculator's default budget).
rubrics.total_yearly_spend: ~$41M distributed in 2024; ~$34.9M in the SFF-2025 round ($33M in 2023, $16M in 2022). Site total: ~$152M coordinated since 2019. 2026 rounds estimate $20–40M.
rubrics.grants_per_year: ~90–100 organizations per year (89 orgs in SFF-2024 round; ~90+ in SFF-2025; Manifund bulletin: "~$30-40m across 100 grants in recent years")
rubrics.process_notes: Decisions run through the **S-Process** ("Simulation"): each round, 4–12 part-time Recommenders (subject-matter experts, many from the rationalist/x-risk community) read applications and build marginal-value functions over funding levels for each org in a simulation app, refined over multiple meetings; an algorithm aggregates the curves (including a "Synthetic Mean Recommender") and allocates each funder's budget. Funders — chiefly Jaan Tallinn — always have final say. The process deliberately favors things at least one Recommender is excited about rather than requiring consensus, so single-champion dynamics matter. Since 2024, rounds run parallel tracks (Main, Freedom, Fairness; 2026 adds Climate, Animal Welfare, and human-enhancement theme rounds). Applications are rolling, but evaluation happens in annual rounds (2026 Main Round: apply by April, recommendations ~September, money by year-end). Every applicant must first receive a **Speculation Grant** to be guaranteed S-Process eligibility (95%+ historically approved): individual Speculators (~dozens of trusted community members, each with ~$400k default budgets from a pool that has grown to ~$20M) can approve fast grants — sometimes within a week — which are retroactively netted against later S-Process recommendations, and Speculators' future budgets rise or fall based on how their picks score in the next round. Eligibility: registered charities almost anywhere, for-profits in US/UK/Canada/Australia under stricter conditions; no unsponsored individuals. There is no stated rubric beyond alignment with the survival-and-flourishing mission and Tallinn's published priorities; matching pledges (e.g. 2:1) are often attached to incentivize other donors.

rubrics.name: Long-Term Future Fund (LTFF)
rubrics.thesis:
The Long-Term Future Fund (part of EA Funds) exists to reduce global catastrophic risks — "especially potential risks from advanced artificial intelligence and pandemics" — and to promote longtermist ideas, on the premise that most humans who will ever exist live in the future. In practice the fund is overwhelmingly an AI-safety funder: technical alignment/interpretability research, AI governance and policy analysis, fieldbuilding and talent pipelines (e.g. SERI MATS, upskilling and career-transition grants), and communications (e.g. Rob Miles, AXRP), with a smaller biosecurity slice. Its self-described comparative advantage is **small grants to individuals, independent researchers, and new projects** — the $5k–$200k checks that larger institutional funders like Open Philanthropy / Coefficient Giving don't handle well — available on a rolling, apply-anytime basis.

LTFF thinks in explicit hits-based, expected-value terms. Fund managers score each application from roughly -5 to +5 (a primary investigator scores, others can weigh in), and grants are funded when the average score clears a funding bar that has historically floated between 2.0 and 2.9 depending on available money. The bar is real: excluding desk rejections, only ~24% of applications were funded in the May 2023–March 2024 period (159/672). Person-project fit, track record, and credible signals of talent and dedication dominate the evaluation — the fund has stated publicly that a "median" application from a smart recent graduate (even an Ivy League one) seeking 6–12 months of independent alignment research is *a bit below* the bar absent exceptional evidence of ability or a strong research plan/mentorship setup.

What they avoid: large organizational grants (they see themselves as complements to, not substitutes for, Open Phil-scale funders), projects with meaningful downside risk (PR risk, capabilities externalities, or net-negative community effects — Habryka in particular weighs downside risk heavily), and vague "raising awareness" projects without a theory of change. They are alert to adverse selection: applicants rejected by other funders get extra scrutiny. Typical funded shapes include 6–12 month independent research stipends, career transitions into safety, PhD/program top-ups, compute, workshops, and small org seed funding. A roleplaying grantmaker should be sympathetic to weird-but-reasoned longtermist bets, generous to strong individual talent, skeptical of unproven applicants asking for large salaries, and inclined to fund partial amounts or shorter timeframes (e.g. 6 months instead of 12) as a de-risking move. Note the fund has been in a transitional period since ~2024–2026 (part-time team totaling ~1 FTE, public grant reporting lapsed after early 2024, new leadership being hired as of April 2026), so capacity for hands-on engagement is low — grants are largely arms-length checks, not active partnerships.

rubrics.typical_check_size: $5k–$200k for nearly all grants (published grants run from $1,500 up to ~$316k for programs like SERI MATS); average grant $34.6k in Mar 2022–Mar 2023 and ~$38k in May 2023–Mar 2024, implying a rough median of ~$25k–$35k

Plus a $2M commitment to the Lightcone Commons round in 2026.
rubrics.grants_per_year: ~100–200/year recently (141 grants in May 2023–Mar 2024; 263 in Mar 2022–Mar 2023 at peak funding)
rubrics.process_notes: Rolling applications via a short web form (Paperform, ~1 hour to complete), no deadlines; expedited review available for time-sensitive asks. Each application gets a primary investigator among the part-time fund managers who scores it from -5 to +5; other managers can add scores, and the grant is funded if the average clears the current funding bar (historically 2.0–2.9, moving with available donations — the fund is donation-dependent and has been openly funding-constrained). Acceptance rate ~24% excluding desk rejections. Decision speed has been a known weakness: median ~29 days, mean ~54 days as of 2023, against a stated aim of responding within weeks. What they say they look for: person-project fit, track record and credible talent signals, a concrete theory of change for reducing existential risk (especially from AI), and cost-effectiveness relative to marginal grants at their current bar; they frequently fund less than the requested amount or a shorter duration. Team is all part-time (~1 FTE total); public grant reporting lapsed after early 2024 and the fund announced in April 2026 it is hiring new leadership.

rubrics.name: Coefficient Giving — Technical AI Safety
rubrics.thesis:
Coefficient Giving (renamed from Open Philanthropy in 2025) is by far the largest funder in AI safety — roughly $400M across AI safety in 2025, with ~$1B expected across catastrophic risks in 2026 — and its Technical AI Safety (TAIS) program is the empirical-ML arm of the Navigating Transformative AI fund. The team takes short timelines seriously: they expect near-human-level LLM agents plausibly within a few years and frame their grantmaking around two explicit motivations: (1) safety techniques for near-human-level LLM agents that will be widely deployed with real economic and governmental influence, and (2) techniques that could remain robust as capabilities scale to superintelligence, where they believe most current methods (RLHF, control protocols, oversight) will break down. The central threat model is misalignment — AIs accidentally developing drives or goals their developers didn't intend, combined with developers' demonstrated inability to make models reliably follow safety specifications.

Their 2025 TAIS RFP (~$40M deployed, with capacity to go substantially higher) defines 21 research areas in five clusters, and the starred priorities reveal the taste: adversarial ML (jailbreaks and unintentional misalignment, control evaluations, backdoors/alignment stress tests, alternatives to adversarial training), sophisticated LLM misbehavior (alignment faking experiments, encoded reasoning in chain-of-thought), model transparency (especially *applications* of white-box/interpretability techniques to realistic tasks, not interpretability for its own sake), and white-box estimation of rare misbehavior. They explicitly hold a *higher* bar for: conceptual/deconfusion work about AI risk, brand-new "moonshots for aligning superintelligence," more transparent architectures, and seed funding for new organizations. Proposals must study LLMs or produce insights plausibly transferable to LLMs. They are scope-sensitive, hits-based givers: comfortable with speculative bets if the expected impact is large, but they want proposals concretely connected to their threat models.

Culturally, the team behaves less like a passive evaluator and more like an active field-builder: grantmakers "don't just evaluate proposals; we elicit them" — they pitch researchers on safety agendas, respond to modest asks by pushing applicants toward more ambitious plans (e.g., turning a $10k compute request into a $1M grant to seed Theorem Labs, a formal-verification startup), and treat funding partly as a way to pull talented ML researchers into safety work. They fund the whole stack: API credits and compute (expedited), 0.5–2 year discrete projects, academic start-up packages for new faculty, general support for research nonprofits/FROs, and (with more diligence) new organizations. Indirect costs are capped at 10%. The bar scales with check size: small grants clear on a short form and one video call; multi-million-dollar grants get extended scrutiny of the team, org structure, and theory of change. A grantmaker roleplaying this funder should be generous toward technically-credible empirical safety work in the starred areas, willing to upsize promising proposals, and notably skeptical of purely conceptual work, non-LLM-relevant research, and capabilities-adjacent projects without a clear safety story.

rubrics.typical_check_size: $50k–$5M per their TAIS RFP's stated typical range (from API-credit/compute grants up to seed funding for new research orgs); CG-wide grants span $10k–$50M. Median TAIS check plausibly ~$300k–$600k (estimate: ~$40M spread across the 2025 TAIS grant cohort).
rubrics.total_yearly_spend: TAIS program: ~$40M in 2025 (per team member Jake Mendel, Nov 2025), up from ~$50M committed to technical AI safety research in 2024, and projected >$140M in 2026. Coefficient-wide AI safety: ~$400M in 2025 (Manifund AIS Funder Bulletin).
rubrics.grants_per_year: Navigating Transformative AI fund: 184 grants in 2025 (Manifund bulletin), out of 333 grants / $543M lifetime since 2017 (Longterm Wiki). TAIS is a subset — roughly dozens of grants/year in 2025, with grant volume roughly tripling into 2026 alongside team headcount.
rubrics.process_notes: Entry point is a 300-word Expression of Interest (EOI), evaluated rolling with responses targeted within ~2 weeks; promising EOIs get invited to a full proposal covering research plan, org structure, timeline, and budget. Small grants close on the written materials plus a short video call; larger grants require further discussion, with decisions targeted within ~2 months of a full proposal (awards conditional on legal due diligence; indirect costs capped at 10% of directs). They tell applicants to have a low bar for submitting, accept multiple EOIs per person, and use "revise and resubmit." They prioritize their 21 published research areas — starred topics (jailbreaks, control evaluations, alignment stress tests, alignment-faking experiments, encoded reasoning, applications of white-box techniques, white-box estimation of rare misbehavior) get enthusiasm; daggered topics (conceptual risk clarification, superintelligence-alignment moonshots, transparent architectures) and new-org seed funding face an explicitly higher bar. Work must be LLM-relevant, and applicants may be asked to connect proposals to the team's two threat-model motivations. Grantmakers actively elicit and upsize proposals rather than only evaluating what arrives; historically most CG grants were sourced through internal research and networks rather than open applications, with RFPs (TAIS, capability evaluations, AI governance, capacity-building, career transition) as the open-door channels.
